'''Keith Stewartson''' (20 September 1925 – 7 May 1983) was an English mathematician and fellow of the [[Royal Society]].<ref>Lighthill, M. J. (1985). Keith Stewartson, 20 September 1925-7 May 1983.</ref>

==Early life==
The youngest of three children, Stewartson was born to an English baker in 1925. He was raised in [[Billingham]], [[County Durham]], where he attended [[Stockton Secondary School]], and went to [[St Catharine's College, Cambridge]] in 1942. He won the [[Drury Prize]] in 1943 for his work in the [[Mathematical Tripos]].<ref name=mcs>{{cite web|title=Keith Stewartson Biography|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Stewartson.html|website=www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk|publisher=School of Mathematics and Statistics University of St Andrews, Scotland|access-date=1 July 2015}}</ref><ref name=lifework>{{cite journal|last1=Stuart|first1=J T|authorlink=J. T. Stuart|title=Keith Stewartson: His Life and Work|journal=Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics|date=January 1986|volume=18|issue=1|pages=1–15|doi=10.1146/annurev.fl.18.010186.000245|bibcode=1986AnRFM..18....1S|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Career==
After graduation, with the Second World War still on-going, Stewartson began employment with the [[Ministry of Aircraft Production]]. During his time there he studied compressible [[fluid flow]] problems. After the war he returned to Cambridge and received the [[Mayhew Prize]] in 1946. He resumed research under the guidance of [[Leslie Howarth]] on [[boundary layer theory]]. His research led to his first publication, "Correlated incompressible and compressible boundary layers", which was published by the Royal Society in 1949. He received his doctorate the same year and became a lecturer at [[Bristol University]] in 1950. In 1953 he went to the United States to become a lecturer at the [[California Institute of Technology]] for a year before returning to Bristol University. In 1958 he was awarded a [[Chair (academia)|chair]] at the [[University of Durham]]. After finding Durham University too conservative, he moved to [[University College, London]] in 1964. In his time there, he studied rotating [[fluid flows]], [[shear layers]], [[magnetohydrodynamics]], [[triple-deck theory]], and [[Reynolds number]]. He played major role in the founding of [[Institute of Mathematics and its Applications]] along with [[James Lighthill]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ima.org.uk/about-us/history/origins-of-the-institute/|title = Origins of the Institute}}</ref> In his career he authored 186 papers.<ref name=mcs /><ref name=lifework/>

Natural convection boundary-layers along horizontal plate also known as the indirect convection was first explained by Stewartson in 1958.<ref>Stewartson, K. (1958). On the free convection from a horizontal plate. Zeitschrift für angewandte Mathematik und Physik ZAMP, 9(3), 276-282.</ref>

===Books===
* {{cite book|author=Keith Stewartson|title=The theory of laminar boundary layers in compressible fluids|year=1964|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0198535041}}

==Personal life==
Stewartson was known as a passionate [[rower]] and enjoyed [[theatre]] and [[opera]]. In 1950, he married Jean Forrester; they had three children. In 1965, he became a member of the Royal Society. In 1974, he suffered a [[heart attack]] which he recovered from, before suffering a subsequent one in 1983 which hospitalized him.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aprender-mat.info/ingles/historyDetail.htm?id=Stewartson |title=Keith Stewartson |website=www.aprender-mat.info |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170820034448/http://www.aprender-mat.info/ingles/historyDetail.htm?id=Stewartson |archive-date=2017-08-20}}</ref> Two weeks later he had a third heart attack which proved fatal.<ref name=mcs /><ref name=lifework/>
